tagline.text: A multi-tier waterfall canyoning climb in a limestone gorge in Samboan, southwest Cebu

budget.label: Budget
budget.text: About ₱300–1,200 (per person, including entrance fee and transport)

children.text: Aguinid Falls is a multi-tier waterfall in Barangay Tangbo, Samboan, in southwest Cebu. Locals count eight levels, and the main draw is a canyoning-style adventure with guides: climbing ropes and rock walls and swimming in the river pools.

Aguinid Falls sits in Barangay Tangbo in the municipality of Samboan, at the far southwestern edge of Cebu island facing the Tañon Strait. Along the Tangbo River, waterfalls and small pools climb like stairs through a limestone gorge, and locals divide them into eight levels (Level 1–8). The English Wikipedia article on Samboan describes five tiers, so the number of levels varies from source to source. The difference seems to come from the fact that most visitors only climb Levels 1–5. The water is said to have a pale jade color because of the lime dissolved in the Tangbo River.

What sets this place apart from other Cebu waterfalls is that it is a waterfall you climb, not just one you look at. At the entrance you receive a helmet, life vest, and water shoes, and you head up the river with two guides. You wade through knee-deep water, pull yourself up limestone slopes on ropes, jump from a rock into a pool if you like, and soak in cave-like hollows. Where the canyoning at Kawasan Falls goes down the gorge, here you climb the falls one by one, so the experience feels very different.

Samboan is said to have about 11-12 waterfalls, but reports and local guides say only 3 of them (Aguinid, Binalayan and Dao) are open to the public (this is not an official figure, so confirm locally). Aguinid is the best known, and many people visit it as a day trip combined with whale shark watching in Oslob or a Moalboal itinerary. It is far from the queue-and-photo atmosphere of Kawasan Falls, and many reviews say it is relatively quiet thanks to its small-scale operation. Visitor numbers have been growing in recent years, though, so on weekends and holidays it is best to go early in the morning.

This guide compares travel guides and local-government-related reports published between 2022 and 2026. Fees, which levels are open, and operating days often change from year to year, so treat the figures below only as a guideline, and check the latest announcements with Samboan's tourism office or your local accommodation before you leave.

Waterfalls and pools follow one another from Level 1 to Level 8 along the Tangbo River. Most visitors climb up to Level 5, while Levels 6–8 are more demanding and, according to some guides, you must tell your guide in advance to go there.

At Level 2 you climb an almost vertical limestone slope while holding a rope. Some descriptions put the slope at about 45 degrees, so you use both arms and legs. The guide shows you where to place your feet and pulls you up if needed.
At Level 4 there is a spot where you can jump from a rock into the pool below. Reviews give the height differently, as about
2 m
or about 10 feet, and jumping is optional. If it feels scary, you can skip it by following your guide's advice.

blocks.title: Cave and small cove at Level 5

children.text: Level 5, where most tours end, is considered the most beautiful section. Jade-colored water collects in cave-like rock hollows and a small cove, making it a good place to rest and take photos.

From Level 6 you climb rock walls without ropes, Level 7 means climbing against the current, and Level 8 is said to have the best view. The risk is high, so the upper levels are mostly open to experienced groups and may be closed at certain times, so follow the instructions on site.
Many reviews say it is less commercialized and has fewer visitors than Kawasan Falls. Instead of crowds in front of the falls, it feels more like a small group slowly climbing with a guide.

Two guides lead a team, usually guiding 5–10 people. Many guides also take photos for you, so it is easy to keep a record even without a waterproof camera. Guides are mandatory here, so the rule is never to climb on your own.
Take a bus bound for Bato from the Cebu South Bus Terminal in Cebu City. Check that it is a route via Barili, and tell the driver to drop you off in Samboan or at the Aguinid junction.
Get off in central Samboan or near the Aguinid signpost. One guide says the habal-habal (motorcycle taxi) ride to the entrance takes about
10–15 minutes
At the registration area, pay the
entrance fee and receive a helmet, life vest, and water shoes. You can leave non-waterproof belongings and valuables with the staff.

Start climbing from Level 1 with the two guides. Pass the rope sections, the rest pools, and the jump point, then rest and take photos at Level 5. Reviewers who climbed slowly and took photos reported about
1.5–2 hours
Come back down the way you went up, or walk down along a path beside the river. One review says the walking path takes about
10 minutes
Have a snack and a drink at the stalls near the entrance, and change out of your wet clothes. Eat lunch in central Samboan and take the bus back.

The bus from Cebu City to Samboan takes about 3–4 hours, so a day trip from Cebu City makes for a full day. If you want a more relaxed schedule, stay a night in Samboan, Oslob, or Moalboal and go early in the morning.

items.title: From Samboan to the falls entrance

children.text: From central Samboan it takes about
10–15 minutes
by habal-habal or tricycle. We found no source for the fare, so agree on a price before you ride.
You can also rent a scooter and ride yourself. Some reviews report renting one in Moalboal or Samboan for about
per day (fuel included). However, the coastal road has heavy traffic and an international driving permit is required, so consider your own riding ability.

The dry season from December to May is the safest time to visit Aguinid Falls. February to May in particular is hot and dry, so the cold river water is welcome, and the rocks are less slippery because the gorge is drier. Some reviews may mention a weaker flow toward late May, so ask about recent conditions.

In the rainy season from June to November, heavy rain can make the river rise and become dangerous. Entry may be restricted when it rains a lot, and there are records of other waterfalls in Samboan being closed during heavy rain. If you go in the rainy season, keep your schedule flexible and decide by the weather.

Samboan itself has a few small places to stay, but Oslob and Moalboal offer more choices. Moalboal is about 1 hour 20 minutes from the falls by car, so a common plan is to stay at a beach lodging there and make a day trip. Prices vary a lot by season, so check directly on booking sites.

Reviews mention small stalls near the falls entrance selling snacks and drinks, plus a few souvenir stands. There are not many restaurants, so it is safer to have lunch in central Samboan or to bring snacks and water. There is also a record saying that the Torta de Tangbo in Samboan's Tangbo area is well known in the region.
The entrance fee is around
but it has changed over the years, so bring enough cash. There may not be many ATMs in Samboan.
Bring a waterproof bag or case. One review says you can leave non-waterproof belongings at the ticket counter.
Prepare a change of clothes, a towel, drinking water, and sandals or trekking shoes. Water shoes are provided, but they may not fit, so bring your own if you are more comfortable in them.
Climb one at a time behind the guide, and ask the guide where to hold on as you move.
Jumping is optional. The height is said to be about
2 m
(about 10 feet), but follow the guide's instructions on the pool depth and where to land.
If you want to go to Levels 6–8, tell them in advance when you register. One guide says going from Level 5 to Level 6 means walking a slippery path for about
20 minutes
more.
Buy travel insurance. The rope and rock sections carry a chance of minor injuries.
Entering early in the morning means fewer people and weaker sunlight. Considering the return bus times, finish by early afternoon at the latest.
Reports say accidents and deaths have happened on the upper levels, so a guide is mandatory and you should only climb to the level your guide allows.
Heavy rain makes the river rise and become dangerous. Ask your accommodation or guide about rain the day before and on the day, and give up if it pours.
Limestone rock is very slippery when wet. Avoid going barefoot or in slippers, and always wear the water shoes you are given.
If you have back or knee problems, a strong fear of heights, or a heart condition, do not push yourself. The rope climbing sections can be hard for children and older people.
Levels 6–8 are high-risk and may be closed at certain times. Follow the on-site instructions on how far up you may go that day.
Fees, operating days, and open levels change often. Check the latest announcement.
